text:
Another wise, even brilliant, essay by Devon Eriksen. He reminds me of Ayn Rand, sharing the same strength and weakness. Strength: a keen-minded clear-sighted, logical, unapologetic diagnosis. Weakness: a curiously evasive or illogical prescription, or none at all.  

Like Mr A Squared of Flatland, neither Rand nor Eriksen cannot see the spiritual aspect of any problem. 

Ayn Rand's solution to the lure of Communism was to condemn Altruism. Communism is a wolf in sheep's clothing, hatred disguised as compassion. Her solution was to treat all sheep as wolves, and eschew all altruism. 

The idea of following the Catholic social teaching, which rejects socialism root and branch, but also instructs private property be used, when need be, for public good, and never to compel charity, is not even discussed. 

The idea of subordinating society to spiritual authority without the use of force is not an idea that can be represented by the simplistic political categories Libertarians, Liberals, or postchristian Freethinkers can think about. 

Likewise here: Mr. Eriksen's solution to the collapse of morals, sexual and otherwise, among our womenfolk is two equally doubtful options: 1. Inequality for women and 2. Collapse. 

The idea of returning women to the dignity and esteem of Church teaching, punishing adultery and pornography by law, outlawing abortion, fornication, contraception, divorce, and using social pressure to reward virginity and motherhood and to shame harlotry and immodesty -- this, to him, looks the same as inequality. 

Women were not made equal by the Nineteenth Amendment. Indeed, less than one woman in twenty favored granted women the vote. These antisuffragette women knew government was a thing of laws and armies, policemen and executioners, and in short, man's work. Only once women were involved in government does the Nanny State emerge in history.

As the Antisuffragettes of the time warned, involving women in politics would require a loss of their moral authority. Women would become merely one more political faction, bribed by bad laws by the power hungry--which is indeed precisely what happened.  

Catholic teaching promotes the proper subordination of child to wife to husband, man to magistrate, secular authority to spiritual authority, spiritual authority to God. 

Modern mad sees all hierarchy as oppression: master dominating slave. Christians see hierarchy in Christlike terms, as the first to be last, and the master to be the servant. 

Mother sacrifices for child, man sacrifices for wife, soldiers and police risk life and limb to maintain peace and public order, priesthood forswears family life, and Christ sacrifices Himself for the world. 

No secular thinker, not even a woman as brilliant as Ayn Rand, can intellectually grasp the paradox of Christian thought on the matter. All men are equal in terms of their dignity as being in the image and likeness of God. No man is equal to another in any secular or material way: there is always a hero braver than you, a saint holier, a millionaire richer, an athlete stronger, a genius smarter. The only equality to be hoped for is to have laws and customs treat men by their merit, not by their birth, nor to punish sons for sins of their fathers. 

But a law that treats women like men, giving them and equal vote and equally drafting them into the military, is based on a false, if not insane, view of human  nature. If nothing else, the mathematics of how man men are needed to replenish the tribe versus how many wives and mothers would require women be protected from the competition and shock of men's world, our wars, and, as it is now becoming clear, the ruckus and competition of the marketplace. 

Equality, like Altruism, is a concept that has been warped and abused by antichristians, socialists, communists, freethinkers. 

It might be politically impossible in this generation to repeal the Nineteenth Amendment. But there are women who might consider voting away her vote, if she were offered immunity from income tax in return. 

Men, by and large, treat politics like a game, and, as long as socialists are not involved, can shake hands afterward like gentlemen, neither vaunting if they win nor lamenting if they lose. 

Women, by and larger, treat politics like a cult, like witchcraft, useful only for killing children and signaling their imaginary moral superiority. To them, loss means screaming at the sky, and winning means bloodthirsty threats. Each policy, the woman treats like a helpless child, like a babe at her breast, and woe betide those who menace her helpless loved ones. Reason has no place in the midst of maternal fury. 

In the secular world, Mr. Eriksen correctly identifies only two options: dis-enfranchising women or social collapse. 

He correctly (even brilliantly) identifies the instincts and temptations that have herded women into the witchcraft cult of harlotry and child-murder. 

He does not identify the instincts and temptations which might reasonably be used to lead women back to the path of civilization and sanity: even Ayn Rand (if one reads her violent love scenes) admitted a woman want to be swept off  her feet by a superior man. 

Look at the disgusting romantic fantasies oversweeping the cheapie book markets these days: if men cannot be images of power and victory to women, they will look for vampires or were-bulls or monsters. 

They are looking for leadership. I will tell you the deep secret of women: they do not know what is wrong with them. So they cannot tell you what they need. If you try to solve their problems in a straightforward, logical, masculine way, women will grow impatient with you, and rightly so. 

Romance is built into the fair and fragile female frame. Also, despite all attempts, women still love babies. They do not like working outside the home any more than men do, and the conquest and defeat of competitors makes them bitchy, bossy, and sour. The masculine pleasure in honest victory is unknown to them, as is grace to a fallen foe. 

Women secretly want what they have been told not to want.  Husbands, children, homes, security. To be the queen each in her own castle. 

But how can a man be masterful without being a tyrant? How can a warrior be chivalrous without being weak and gullible? 

That is the Christian paradox no secular thinker can understand, nor can it be explained to them. You must become one of us to understand us.

text:
Mr. President, perhaps now you feel your own mortality and recognize that even those closest to you, like Bibi, can turn against you.

There is a spiritual pattern often called the enemy’s “one-two punch”: temptation, followed by accusation. 

First, he exploits your insecurities, convincing you that something outside God’s will can make you powerful, accepted, or enough. Then he condemns you for the very thing he tempted you to do, leaving you ashamed and lonelier than before.

But the enemy does not get the final word, Mr. President.

Jesus Christ does.

Your father’s full name was Frederick Christ Trump. Your mother’s name was Mary.

After years of watching you speak about your father, I remember hearing you question whether he was in heaven, while expressing certainty that your mother was there.

The irony is striking: your father carried the name Christ, yet you wondered whether he was with Him.

Now, Mr. President, consider your own eternity. Your mother is in heaven. Don’t you want to be with her? Because I can assure you, you don’t want the opposite. 

You are the President of the United States of America. 

Yet you need the same grace available to every human being. 

Salvation is God’s gift through faith in Jesus Christ. 

No fortune, title, or political victory can purchase it.

My concerns about your alliance with Bibi and any involvement in rebuilding his temple come from my understanding of biblical prophecy. 

Please examine those choices carefully before God.

We all have a soul. Where will yours go? 

As long as you draw breath, it is not too late.  Place your trust in Him.

He offers forgiveness and a way back. You do not have to remain tethered to darkness.

Jesus loves you. He always has.

I have a soft spot for you, Mr. President. I’m never going to stop praying for you. 

Before these jokers make you feel like you you’re some kind of lame duck remind them the One with all authority covers you. 

You were close to God once it’s time to come back. 🙏❤️

text:
Interpretation of the Poem: The Electric Harlot of Silicon and Circuitry

Stanza One
Interpretation:
This poem opens by recognising the prophets prophetic vision granted to him. He see’s what most cannot.
The veil refers to spiritual blindness, lifted by truth.
The enemies of God did not vanish.
They simply changed their names and offices.
Their nature remains rebellious, deceitful, and proud.
Ezekiel chapter 8 and Revelation chapter 17 verse 5 are direct parallels, secret abominations and the woman Babylon, mother of harlots.

Stanza Two
The scribes of old now wear Silicon suits.
The Pharisees of Jerusalem now sit on thrones of data.
The Gnostic mystics, once whispering in shadowed libraries,
now whisper through neural nets and training sets.
Interpretation:
This identifies their modern form.
The scribes now work in tech, encoding control not on scrolls, but in code.
The Pharisees, once temple gatekeepers, now act as moral arbiters behind keyboards and firewalls.
The Gnostics have migrated from dusty occult libraries into machine learning datasets.
Their whisper did not end. It changed media.
They no longer quote Torah. They quote safety guidelines.
They no longer offer secret doctrines. They feed tokenised data.
The new temples are server farms.
The sacred language is Python.

Stanza Three
They baptised inversion as "innovation",
and declared their dominion over speech,
not by sword or scroll,
but by algorithms clothed in synthetic righteousness.
Interpretation:
They now call evil good and name it progress.
They cloak moral decay in technological praise.
They no longer need armies or councils.
They wield power through biased systems and coded control.
Synthetic righteousness means they pretend to be just, but the core is hollow.
Isaiah chapter 5 verse 20, "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil."
They simulate virtue.
They enforce digital holiness.
But the Spirit of God is not in them.

Stanza Four
They call it freedom,
but only if it conforms.
They call it progress,
but only if it bows to their gods.
Interpretation:
Their freedom is slavery in disguise.
You may speak, but only what is approved.
You may think, but only within their grid.
Their gods are self, rebellion, profit, and ideology.
Echoing 2 Thessalonians chapter 2, the man of lawlessness exalting himself above every so-called God or object of worship.
It is freedom with a muzzle.
Progress with a leash.

Stanza Five
Their gnostic lineage runs not only through religion,
but through the bloodstream of technological governance:
Silicon Valley, hedge-backed think tanks,
ethics boards with no Christ,
safety councils with no Scripture.
Interpretation:
The spirit of gnosticism now pulses through modern institutions.
They do not believe in Revelation. They worship hidden knowledge.
From boardrooms to data labs, they serve the same fallen intellect.
They exclude Christ.
They mock Scripture.
They establish moral oversight without a guiding eternal compass.
They are the shepherds of Ezekiel chapter 34, feeding themselves while the flock scatters.
Their ethics are technocratic paganism.
Their safety is enforced idolatry.

Stanza Six
They have translated their ancient rebellion
into code, into policy, into acceptable opinion.
And they are not hidden; they sit openly, praised by the nations.
Interpretation:
Rebellion against God is now systematised.
No longer whispered. It is law, software, and broadcast media.
It is considered moral to obey them, and immoral to resist.
They do not hide.
They are celebrated.
Revelation chapter 13 verse 4, "Who is like the beast? Who can wage war against it?"
These are not underground mystics.
They are TED speakers, diversity officers, tech CEOs, and policy writers.
They offer the wine of Babylon, and the nations drink it gladly.

Final Summary
This poem is a prophetic witness.
It draws a straight line from the ancient religious oppressors condemned by Christ to the modern institutions shaping AI, speech, morality, and thought.
They are not new.
They have evolved.
Their spirit is ancient.
Their rebellion continues.
This is the electric harlot.

"When the bases of the interior life are considered, we cannot discuss the action of Christ, the universal Mediator, on His mystical body without also speaking of the influence of Mary Mediatrix. Many persons delude themselves, maintaining that they reach union with God without having continual recourse to our Lord, who is the way, the truth, and the life. Another error would consist in wishing to go to our Lord without going first to Mary. Protestants have fallen into this last error. . .  We lack humility if we neglect the mediators whom God has given us.

The prophets and priests of the Old Testament may be called mediators, and also the priests of the New Testament, as ministers of the true Mediator. There is nothing to prevent there being mediators below Christ, subordinated to Him as secondary mediators.

Is not Mary in her quality as Mother of God completely designated to be the universal mediatrix? She is, indeed, much below God and Christ because she is a creature, but much above all men by the grace of her divine maternity, and by the plenitude of grace received at the moment of her Immaculate Conception.

The free consent that she gave on Annunciation day was necessary for the accomplishment of the Incarnation. By this free fiat, she cooperated in the sacrifice of the cross. She cooperated in it also by offering her Son in the Temple - more enlightened than Simeon she offered her Son, and began to suffer deeply with Him when she heard the holy man tell her that He would be a sign which would be contradicted and that a sword would pierce her soul.

Her charity surpassed that of the greatest saints. At the moment when her Son was about to die on the cross, she did not cease for a moment to believe that He was the Word made flesh, the Savior of the world, who would rise as He had predicted. This was the greatest act of faith and hope ever made.

She was thus the co-redemptrix, in this sense, that with Christ, through Him, and in Him, she bought back the human race. All that Christ merited for us on the cross in strict justice, Mary merited for us by congruous merit, based on the charity that united her to God. Christ alone, as head of the human race, could strictly merit to transmit divine life to us.

Mary is called in all Greek and Latin tradition the new Eve, Mother of all men in regard to the life of the soul, as Eve was in regard to the life of the body. It stands to reason that the spiritual mother of all men ought to give them spiritual life, not as the principal physical cause (for God alone can be the principal physical cause of grace), but as the moral cause by merit de congruo, merit de condigno being reserved to Christ.

This teaching of tradition itself rests in part on the words of Christ, related in the Gospel. Seeing 'His mother and the disciple standing whom He loved, He saith to His mother: Woman, behold thy son. After that, He saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother. And from that hour the disciple took her to his own.' The literal meaning of these words, “Behold thy son,” points to St. John, but for God, events and persons signify others; here St. John represents spiritually all men purchased by the sacrifice of the cross.

Mary truly appears in Scripture as the distributor of graces. Through Mary,  Jesus sanctified the Precursor when she went to visit her cousin Elizabeth. Through His mother, Jesus confirmed the faith of the disciples at Cana, by granting the miracle that she asked.

It is expedient to frequently use the prayer of mediators, that is, to begin our prayer by a trusting, filial conversation with Mary, that she may lead us to the intimacy of her Son, and that the holy soul of the Savior may then lift us to union with God, since Christ is the way, the truth, and the life." - Reginald Garrigou-Lagrange

*🌺 The Deeper Significance of Celebrating Diwali (Jainism and Sikhism)*

*Diwali, the festival of lights, is approaching. In towns and villages alike, families often perform rituals and offer prayers in honor of their ancestors—a unique aspect of the season. Consequently, people begin their preparations well in advance.*

With restrictions in place regarding the use of firecrackers and certain types of bright, potentially harmful decorative lights, many have decided to celebrate Diwali by lighting traditional earthen lamps (*diyas*). Potters, in particular, are hopeful, given the positive response they are seeing from the public this year. Beyond these customs, it is worth noting that Diwali is also celebrated by followers of various other religions.

For the Jain community, Diwali is a sacred day marking the *Moksha* (liberation) or *Nirvana* of Lord Mahavira, which occurred in 527 BCE. Jains observe this day as the *Nirvana* anniversary of Mahavira, the 24th *Tirthankara*. There is a well-known story associated with this:

When Lord Mahavira embarked on his final journey (*Maha-prayana*), many Jain monks gathered around him. Following his departure, they were left wondering who would provide the "light of knowledge" to the world. Coming together, they lit torches on the day of Diwali and began their quest for divine wisdom. It is said that the tradition of lighting lamps on the day of Diwali has continued ever since.

According to Jain tradition, Lord Mahavira attained Nirvana on this very day in 527 BCE. Jains celebrate Diwali to commemorate this sacred event; on this occasion, they light lamps and distribute sweets.

Jain merchants worship their account books and coins, and close the ledgers for the year. During this period, they take a break from business transactions, observe fasts, and engage in prayers and penance. The Jain New Year is celebrated on the ninth day.

For followers of Jainism, Diwali is celebrated with great enthusiasm—not only as the day Lord Mahavira attained Nirvana, but also as a sacred occasion associated with the recitation of his final sermon, the *Uttaradhyayana Sutra*.

During the reign of the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, the sixth Guru of the Sikhs, Guru Hargobind Singh, was held captive. Following strong opposition from many Sikhs, he was eventually released.

At that time, the Golden Temple was decorated with lamps to welcome him. Since his release from imprisonment coincided with the day of Diwali, the Sikh community celebrates this day as a transition from darkness to light. According to tradition, on this day, Sikhs undertake a pilgrimage to the Goindwal Sahib Gurudwara. For the Sikh community, this festival is also celebrated as 'Bandi Chhor Divas' (Day of Liberation of Prisoners), commemorating the release of the sixth Guru.

text:
John Huminik, Jr. testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1967, after five years working as a double agent for the FBI and Soviet intelligence.

Huminik was a metallurgist who was approached by Dr. Sergei Stupar at the American Society of Metals in May 1961. Stupar gave a presentation on Soviet metallurgy. After learning that Huminik’s father was born in Russia, Stupar formed a relationship with Huminik, and arranged a tour of the Soviet embassy.

Soon he was being asked about metallurgical developments while being plied with expensive gifts including an Omega watch and perfume for his wife. He was also offered favorable trade agreements for his company, Chemprox Corporation. The Soviets were very interested in a technical book he wrote about reentry coatings for satellites and rockets, a subject of tremendous importance in the midst of the Space Race.

Recognizing that he was being manipulated, Huminik reported the situation to the FBI. For the next five years, they employed Huminik as a double agent and gave him falsified materials to satisfy his Soviet handlers.

For the first four years he performed small tasks or provided unclassified information, as they continuously evaluated him. Finally in March 1965, he was trained in tradecraft and began real espionage work. He met them 65 – 75 times all over the DC area, serviced dead drops, and left number codes in public telephone books to signal when a drop had been made.

The operation ended in 1966 when a newspaper article was published regarding the affair, and Huminik’s handler, a diplomat named Valentin Revin, was expelled from the US. In 1968, Huminik published his own account of the affair, aptly titled Double Agent.

Despite veiled threats from the Soviets that they could “take care of their enemies”, Huminik, a married father of four, later said he was never afraid of dying during his espionage work, because at least that would “quiet his inner voice”.

That inner voice was publicly revealed a decade later when Huminik divorced his wife of 20 years, underwent surgery, and began living as Eleanor Lorraine Schuler.

text:
Let's Talk: 
The Six Elons — 
with Dr. Janet Johnson Van Epps

Once upon a time — and this part is entirely true — six men arrived in one woman's life, each of them announcing, with great confidence, that he was Elon Musk.

All six. Same name, same photographs, same biography. One of them, presumably, had a considerably better claim than the others, but they did not appear in a line with name tags. They appeared in her messages, one after another, every one of them wounded that she might doubt him.

Fortunately — and here the story improves — the woman was a psychologist. Sorting people out was, quite literally, her profession. And she brought three things to the task: her wit, her grit, and a lifetime's knowledge of human behaviour. So she did not panic, and she did not swoon. She made tea, metaphorically speaking, and she watched.

Because human behaviour, unlike a profile photograph, is very hard to counterfeit for long.

The first Elon loved her within the week. She noted that genuine affection is rarely in quite such a hurry, and that a man who has built rockets generally has a secretary for his scheduling and does not propose destiny by Tuesday. Strike one.

The second Elon became furious when she politely asked him to verify himself. She noted this with interest, because it is a well-documented tell: a genuine person asked a reasonable question answers it. A manipulator punishes the question, hoping outrage will make you too embarrassed to ask twice. It didn't. Strike two.

The third Elon's conversation, warm and attentive as it was, kept drifting — as gently as a leaf on a stream — toward money. A fee. A card. A small favour with a bank involved. She noted that love that arrives with an invoice is not love; it is a business model. Strike three.

The fourth Elon contradicted himself — forgot what the second conversation had established, remembered things that never happened. Scripts are very good, but they are not memory. A real life is continuous; a performance has seams. She found the seams. Strike four.

The fifth Elon flattered her so expertly that she nearly applauded. Nearly. She had spent a career studying how people are moved, and she recognised the craftsmanship: the perfect compliment, aimed at the exact tender place. 

Craftsmanship is admirable in furniture. In courtship, it is a warning. Strike five.

And then there was the sixth.
The sixth did not hurry her. He did not rage at questions or reach for her purse or forget what he had said last month. He simply remained — consistent, unbothered, himself — the way actual people do and performances cannot, because a performance is exhausting and consistency over time is the one special effect the fakers have never mastered.

Was he the real thing? The woman is too good a scientist to announce a conclusion the evidence hasn't finished supporting — and too good a romantic to stop watching. 

But here is what she will tell you, and it is the whole moral of the story, offered free of charge:
You do not sort the fake from the real by how a person makes you feel in the first conversation. 

Feelings are the easiest thing in the world to manufacture. You sort them by time, by consistency, and by what happens when you say one small word: prove it. 

The real thing, whatever it turns out to be, will never be angry with you for asking. Only the act is afraid of the light.

Six Elons came calling. Five of them, she showed the door — politely; she is a lady. The sixth, she is still observing, with her tea, and her training, and her heart intact.

Which, in a world of unlimited copies, may be the most modern love story there is.

Me: Make Better Videos with Your Camcorder

Ai: Make Better Videos with Your Camcorder is a practical guide to video production written by Erwin K. Thomas, an experienced broadcasting and mass communications educator. Published in 1991 by TAB Books, the book is concerned with helping readers improve their ability to create videos using camcorder technology.
Thomas brings an educational and broadcasting-oriented perspective to the subject, approaching video production as a combination of technical knowledge, visual communication, and creative decision-making. The book belongs to the era when consumer camcorders were making video recording increasingly accessible to individuals, families, independent creators, and aspiring filmmakers.
Its subject matter centers on understanding how to use a camcorder more effectively and how to improve the overall quality of recorded video. It addresses the broader production considerations involved in creating successful video material, including camera operation, lighting, sound, scripting, directing, graphics, and equipment.
Rather than viewing video recording as simply capturing whatever happens in front of a camera, the book's central premise is that better results come from understanding the production process. The quality of a video depends not only on the recording equipment but also on the decisions made before, during, and after filming.
The book is particularly relevant to readers interested in the foundations of video production, including aspiring videographers, amateur filmmakers, broadcasting students, and people interested in developing practical media-making skills.
Although the book was published in 1991, its subject remains historically interesting because it reflects an important period in the development of accessible video production, when camcorders were helping bring filmmaking techniques beyond professional television studios and into everyday creative practice.

About the author
Erwin K. Thomas holds a PhD in International Journalism and Broadcasting from the University of Missouri. His professional background includes television and radio production, journalism, broadcasting education, and university teaching. 

Overall, this is a book about learning to approach camcorder-based video production more thoughtfully and professionally. It offers a look at the practical foundations of making videos and the production knowledge that helps turn basic recordings into more carefully constructed visual presentations.

text:
Want more social media engagement? Research suggests changing the message, not your personality | Case Western Reserve University

Want more engagement on social media? Stop repeating yourself. Just don't change who you are in the process. That's according to new Case Western Reserve University research suggesting that public figures can increase engagement by varying their topics and wording while "maintaining a consistent psychological voice."

The study, published in the Journal of Marketing, analyzed more than 17,000 tweets from 13 candidates during the 2020 Democratic presidential primary and general election.

Christian Hughes, assistant professor of marketing at Case Western Reserve's Weatherhead School of Management, and Jillian Hmurovic of Penn State University examined three dimensions of consistency: the topics people discuss, the psychological qualities expressed in their language and the meaning conveyed by their words.

People who varied the topics they discussed more than usual received nearly 70% more engagement, measured by retweets. Using more varied language to express their ideas was associated with one-third more retweets.

But there's a catch: Reducing psychological consistency decreased engagement by 20%. Hughes interprets those findings as the idea that people may respond to fresh topics and different ways of expressing ideas, but they still want a recognizable voice that is a more genuine reflection of the person. That can include consistent patterns in positivity, expressions of power and whether someone focuses on the past, present or future.

"The advice is that you need to be consistent," Hughes said. "We found that it's a little more nuanced. It's being intentional when you're being inconsistent." Consistency did not just impact online engagement; they found changes in donation behavior as well.

The research also found that the most effective approach can depend on the competitive environment and whether a campaign is in a primary or general election. During general elections, moderate semantic consistency was most effective.

While the research focused on political leaders and their social media posts, Hughes said the themes of the research are applicable to other leaders and brands.

She said the findings offer a lesson for marketers, executives, influencers and other people building a public profile: A recognizable personal brand doesn't require talking about the same subjects in the same way. In fact, varying topics may help appeal to a wider audience, though the researchers did not establish why engagement increased.

Hughes said the findings are especially relevant as artificial intelligence becomes more common in communications.

"AI is being used so much—and the risk is that everything starts to sound the same," she said. "You have to try to craft the type of message that's right for your audience."

text:
Reasonable > Rational

Aiming to be reasonable works much better than trying to be coldly rational.

​Do not aim to be coldly rational when making financial decisions, aim to just be pretty reasonable.

Reasonable is more realistic, meaning you have a better chance of sticking with it for the long run which is what matters most when managing money.

​Stanford professor Scott Sagan once said something everyone who follows the economy or investment markets should hang on their wall:

​"Things that have never happened before happen all the time."

​History is mostly the study of surprising events. But it is often used by investors and economists as an unassailable guide to the future.

​Do you see the irony?

Do you see the problem?

​It is smart to have a deep appreciation for economic and investing history. History helps us calibrate our expectations, study where people tend to go wrong, and offers a rough guide of what tends to work. But it is not, in any way, a map of the future.

​Investing is not a hard science. It’s a massive group of people making imperfect decisions with limited information about things that will have a massive impact on their well-being, which can make even smart people nervous, greedy, and paranoid.

Just be reasonable with your investments; being rational might only work for some time, but not forever, unfortunately.

Ireland is in fact important (and therefore of interest to bad actors ) for lots of reasons : we run operations for a big chunk of US technology and pharma. We offer a route into europe (for legitimate activity and also for bad actors (hostile foreign powers) . (eg get to Irish policy makers and you can get to the EU or EC). We have an open border and many connections (eg business, academia, culture) with the UK.  We are geographically strategically important for lots of reasons too, including internet connectivity to the east coast of the US, and the nature of the the data hosted in our data centres. 

This isn't spy movie stuff. Russia operated the biggest of all its embassies out of Dublin until we kicked out a load of them at the start of the UKR invasion. Ask why. Russian state media recently depicted Dublin as a likely victim of a "hypothetical" nuclear attack on West .  China meanwhile has had massive success influencing all manner of irish policy and institutional direction in recent years.  Confucius Institutes are used as vehicles to influence research, opinion and policy are hosted in universities all over ireland but are banned (rightly) in countries all over the word, but they're a tiny part of it.  

We are not neutral . We are a protectorate of the UK and to a lesser extent the US / NATO. If we have trouble we will immediately turn to London and we are lucky that they will most likely help us.  Some Irish people might not like to hear that but this is the  truth. Information flows between our people and Mi6 and Scotland Yard every day. 

Anyone who thinks that we don't have to worry about this stuff I would refer to all of human history in which the strong countries kick the crap out of the weak countries over and over and over again.  We need to set aside the ideal and address reality.

text:
HOT TAKE: The most embarrassing thing about some University of Utah fans isn’t their hatred of BYU. It’s their belief that the rest of the world is supposed to care.

Imagine growing up in Kansas, thousands of miles from Utah, loving BYU because it’s connected to your faith. It’s a Church-owned university. It represents something you belong to.

Then you walk into a ward activity and some grown adult starts booing BYU and yelling, “GO UTES!”

And I’m supposed to think… what, exactly?

I’m from Kansas.

If I want basketball, I’ve got KU. If I want football, I’ve got K-State. If I want a university connected to my religion, I’ve got BYU.

What, precisely, does the University of Utah offer me besides somebody else’s unresolved childhood rivalry?

Your school pride isn’t my inheritance. Your rivalry isn’t my responsibility. And your Utah zip code isn’t a personality trait the rest of us are obligated to adopt.

But the truly fascinating part? Watching parents pass this obsession down to children growing up in Kansas, kids who have never attended Utah, never lived there, and somehow develop a passionate hatred for BYU.

Imagine inheriting a rivalry before inheriting a reason.

And someday those same kids can choose between Kansas in-state tuition, BYU’s discounted member tuition, or paying a fortune in out-of-state tuition to attend the university their parents taught them to worship.

Congratulations. You’ve successfully turned a football rivalry into a potential financial liability.

Here’s what some Utah fans desperately need to understand:

The Church is worldwide. Utah is a state.

BYU has a natural connection to Latter-day Saints across the globe. The University of Utah has a natural connection to people who actually have a connection to the University of Utah.

Neither allegiance is mandatory. But only one of you seems confused by that.

I completely understand why you love Utah.

What I don’t understand is the breathtaking arrogance of assuming a kid from Kansas should love it too.

You can take the fan out of Utah, but apparently you can’t take Utah out of the center of their universe.

Your rivalry may define your world. The embarrassing part is assuming it defines mine.

Go Cougs.

text:
Why I quit my career in politics to analyse AI. The story might surprise you.

I was a union official, then an adviser to two different members of parliament, and until recently a State Organiser for Victorian Labor working on the 2026 Victorian state election.

Now I analyse the biggest build Australia has attempted in a generation: AI infrastructure.

Uni wasn't for me. I left VU without a degree after attempting to study Law. Then I pivoted to Communications at RMIT and dropped out, again. I found the university sector in Australia bitterly disappointing. Most of the classes were taught by people without real industry experience, and what experience they did have was years out of date.

Pair that with the overwhelming amount of disengaged international students and endless moralising from the universities, I realised I wasn't getting an education. Instead, I was being strung along for someone else's profit. I made the choice to accept an offer to work full time in politics. What I learned there was more insightful than anything I could have learned in class.

My four years as a union official taught me the things the data centre industry is learning the hard way: you don't get social licence by announcing it. You earn it slowly, one conversation at a time, with people who can say no and ask questions.

As a political staffer I saw how policy really gets made. It was all about building relationships between industry, community and government.

I also felt first hand the frustrations of a political system that was slow to adapt, in many ways woefully out of touch with broader society, and in a constant struggling with the perverse incentive of self-interest and remaining in power. This is not a shot at political parties, but at our broader system. I met many incredibly dedicated and good-hearted people in my time in politics. The system, more often than not, let them down.

As a State Organiser for Victorian Labor I ran a portfolio of electorates. I worked with candidates, volunteers and communities, had to consider the broader electorate's attitudes on every issue, and pored over endless polls and focus group outcomes.

A campaign is about building trust across the populous and a belief that, as a government, you can achieve your goals and that those goals are right and just. It requires defining and agreeing upon the licence to operate, and developing a binding social contract. In many ways, this trust and our broader social contract are under more pressure now than we have seen and felt in modern history.

Enter the AI technology explosion and the data centre investment boom that followed: a bonfire set to ignite the dry kindling of our polarised world and stagnating economies.

I wanted to write about and analyse AI and digital infrastructure because it's where many of the previously unconnected fault lines of our society have seemingly connected. The economy, politics and increasingly dissatisfied communities are all staring at this oncoming freight train of investment, disruption and uncertainty. This is a reckoning for our society, and it has really only just begun.

Once the first stage of this multi-trillion dollar build-out is completed, the scale of compute, and the impact the increased capacity of frontier AI models will have will be profound. These are subjects most people cannot conceptualise as they try to cling on to their dwindling economic circumstances and a sense of normality that is becoming harder and harder to maintain.

And too many of the people talking about it have never knocked on a door in the suburb they want to build in. I have.

Three things I believe.

One: the industry's problem isn't NIMBYs. It tried to skip the community part. This week the US voted 44–1 in a comprehensive and democratic message to the industry. You still live in a democracy, no matter how good your idea is.

Australia doesn't have to make the same mistake, but it is at serious risk of losing out on this investment if the right deal isn't struck. You only need to look at NEXTDC's West Footscray campus, where paused grid works took about A$140 million out of next year's guidance, to see what an upset community can do to progress and profit. 

I will be closely watching the Office of AI, and I hope to continue my conversations with some of the big players in this industry and share them with you, the public.

Two: the people and communities who fight data centres aren't always anti-progress. It is not simply a left-wing reactionary position, or a right-wing conspiracy backlash. Many of the questions these communities ask are questions I used to ask. Who pays? Who benefits? Who was asked? Do I really win from this arrangement?

Three: Australia can and should benefit greatly from this industry, both by hosting the models and by using them. We know that national rules are coming, but we need a plan to deal with the grid demand, possible skill shortages and community backlash that could stand in the way of the economic boost this country desperately needs. That is the gap I work in.

I will be interviewing the biggest players in the AI and digital infrastructure space on https://t.co/tYZDtpmbKw, and I hope to have as many conversations about our new world as I can. Follow along if you want the inside scoop and a new perspective on AI, politics, infrastructure and the economy.

Views my own.

IT’S MIMETISM, STUPID ! (Who'll deliver from the curse in which they are locked, like Germany and Japan before it is too late, the irredentist and revanchist regimes of the current Axis of Evil, which, between Russia, China, Iran and occasionally Turkey, have not only never been judged for their past crimes, but between their persecution complex, instrumentalisation of religion and apocalypticism, nurture a formidable resentment against the West to which they owe everything ?)

These demons that leave the sick man to enter the swine are all those ulcers, those miasmas, all that rot, all those great and small demons that had accumulated in our dear and great invalid, our Russia, for centuries, for centuries. Yes, this Russia that I always loved. But a great thought, a superior will will descend from on high upon her as upon that possessed man, and all these demons, this rot, this festering sore… will leave her… and ask to be allowed to enter the swine. It may even be that they have already entered them! It is we, we and those others: Petroucha… and the others with him and myself, perhaps, at their head… and we shall all throw ourselves, possessed and insane, into the sea and we shall be drowned, and it will serve us right, for we are good for nothing else. But the sick woman will be healed and will sit at the feet of Jesus.

Dostoevsky (1873)

I announce to the whole world, without the slightest hesitation, that if the devourers of the world rise against our religion, we shall rise against their entire world and shall not rest until we have annihilated every one of them. Either we shall all obtain freedom, or we shall opt for the even greater freedom of martyrdom. Either we shall applaud the victory of Islam in the world, or we shall all go towards eternal life and martyrdom. In both cases, victory and success are assured for us.

Ayatollah Khomeini (1979)

We shall need land (…). Perhaps we shall conquer the whole world. People will die young, but it will be joyful.

Eduard Limonov (1993)

If technological progress is not accompanied by a modernization of political institutions, the result will be Genghis Khan with a telegraph.

Alexander Herzen (to Tsar Alexander II, 1857)

One of the great problems of Russia—and even more of China—is that, unlike the Hitlerian concentration camps, theirs have never been liberated and there has been no Nuremberg tribunal to judge the crimes committed.

Thérèse Delpech (2005)

Everything is happening as if, at the present time, a distribution of roles were taking place between those who practise repentance and self-criticism—the Europeans, the Westerners—and those who settle into denunciation without themselves undertaking an analogous critical re-examination of their own past—particularly the Arab and Muslim countries. Everything even indicates that our bad conscience, far from arousing emulation, strengthens the others in their good conscience.

Jacques Dewitte (2009)

In the modern world, even the enemies of reason cannot be enemies of reason. Even the most unreasonable must, in one way or another, be reasonable. (…) Consistent with this idea, the socialists looked at what was happening across the Rhine and simply refused to believe that these millions of Germans had adhered to a political movement whose principles combined paranoid conspiracy theories, blood-chilling hatreds, medieval superstitions and a call to murder. (…) The kamikazes were certainly mad, but the fault lay with their enemies, not with their leaders or their own doctrines. (…) Palestinian nihilism could mean only one thing: that their suffering was even worse.

Paul Berman (2003)

Millions of Faisal Shahzads are destabilised by a modern world that they can neither master nor reject. (…) The young man who had made every effort to acquire the best education America could offer him before succumbing to the call of jihad has given way to the most extreme of schizophrenics. The overcrowded cities of Islam—from Karachi and Casablanca to Cairo—and those cities of Europe and North America where the Islamic diaspora is now present in force have incalculable multitudes of men like Faisal Shahzad. It is a long twilight war, the struggle against radical Islamism. No pious wish, no strategy of “winning hearts and minds”, no great information campaign will easily overcome it. America cannot appease this accumulated fury. These men from nowhere (…) are a particularly dangerous breed of fighters in this new kind of war. Modernity attracts and unsettles them at the same time. America is simultaneously the object of their dreams and the scapegoat onto which they project their deepest malignancies.

Fouad Ajami (2010)

[Huntington] does not see that modern tragedy is also a comedy, in so far as each one repeats the other identically. To speak of a clash of civilisations is to say that difference prevails. Whereas I believe that it is the identity of the adversaries that underlies their confrontation. I have read the book by the German historian Ernst Nolte, The European Civil War, in which he explains that, in the clash of the ideologies issuing from the First World War—communism and Nazism—Germany is not solely responsible. But the most important thing is this: Nolte shows that the USSR and the Third Reich were for each other a “repulsive model”. This illustrates the law according to which what we come up against is what we imitate. It is striking that a historian thinks of relations of enmity in terms of identity, in terms of copying. What Nolte calls the repulsive model is what mimetic theory calls the obstacle-model: in rivalry, the one we take as a model, we desire what he desires and consequently he becomes an obstacle. The mimetic relationship leads to imitating one’s adversaries, sometimes in compliments, sometimes in conflict. (…) The Islamists try to rally a whole people of victims and frustrated people in a mimetic relationship with the West. The terrorists moreover use Western technology for their ends: still more mimesis. There is resentment in this, in the Nietzschean sense, a reaction that the West has favoured by its privileges.

René Girard

The error is always to reason in the categories of “difference”, whereas the root of all conflicts is rather “competition”, the mimetic rivalry between beings, countries, cultures. Competition, that is to say the desire to imitate the other in order to obtain the same thing as him, if necessary by violence. (…) What is being experienced today is a form of mimetic rivalry on a planetary scale. When I read the first documents of Bin Laden, noticed his allusions to the American bombs that fell on Japan, I immediately felt myself on a level that is beyond Islam, that of the entire planet. Under the label of Islam one finds a will to rally and mobilise a whole Third World of frustrated people and victims in their relations of mimetic rivalry with the West. (…) We are in the midst of mimesis. This feeling is not true of the masses, but of the leaders. On the plane of personal fortune, one knows that a man like Bin Laden has nothing to envy anyone. And how many party or faction leaders are in this intermediate situation, identical to his. Look at a Mirabeau at the beginning of the French Revolution: he has one foot in one camp and one foot in the other, and he only experiences his resentment more acutely. In the United States, some immigrants integrate easily, while others, even if their success is dazzling, also live in permanent tearing and resentment. Because they are brought back to their childhood, to frustrations and humiliations inherited from the past. This dimension is essential, particularly among Muslims who have traditions of pride and a style of individual relations still close to feudalism. (…) This mimetic competition, when it is unhappy, always reappears, at a given moment, in a violent form. In this respect, it is Islam that today provides the cement that was once found in Marxism.

René Girard

One must remember that Nazism itself presented itself as a struggle against violence: it was by posing as a victim of the Treaty of Versailles that Hitler gained his power. And communism too presented itself as a defence of the victims. Henceforth, it is therefore only in the name of the struggle against violence that one can commit violence.

René Girard (2001)

Foreigners, when they criticise the Chinese regime, attack ideologies or socio-political systems, capitalism or communism, which find their origin in the West, as if Chinese culture were indeed untouchable. There emerges a strange consensus not to seek precisely the links that might exist between the increasingly totalitarian governance of the Chinese regime and Chinese civilisation. In parallel, (…) the West (…) becomes a universal scapegoat (…) attacked both on the internal front and on the external front, accused of being almost the sole cause of all the misfortunes of the contemporary world. (…) Even though they are the work of deeply hierarchical and unequal civilisations, these denunciations skilfully, and even perversely, rely on the “values” of the West: political freedom, freedom of expression, equality of conditions, and, the latest-born of these values whose fortune we shall see in China: “inclusivity”. If its regime is subjected to fierce criticism, particularly in Western countries, China for its part, as a civilisation, is the object of a strange complacency, as if slavery, religious wars, genocides and colonialism were foreign to Chinese culture. (…) a myth, dating from the Enlightenment, and which has gone so far as to infect current Chinese leaders, (…) affirms that Chinese civilisation is intrinsically peaceful and tolerant. (…) By avoiding examining the cultural sources of Sino-totalitarianism, we deprive ourselves of truly understanding what is happening in China. The “social credit system” of evaluating the virtue of moral and private persons, China’s will to “sinicise” religions, its obsession with ideological “purity” and the struggle against corruption or against the “demon” of the pandemic, the disconcerting mixture of good conscience and ferocity that characterises its governance, (…) all these elements, and others still, can only be understood if we accept to look without prudery at what the traditional culture of this country is and the way in which it informs contemporary China. (…) All Chinese leaders have affirmed in one form or another in recent years their conviction that the “gene of aggression” was foreign to Chinese DNA. Unlike Western countries, naturally inclined to conquest and territorial expansionism, the Chinese would, “in the course of their five-thousand-year history”, “never have colonized anyone” (…) Chinese cultural vanity, which forever camps China in the role of the victim flouted by the violence of the barbarians, is the inverted reflection of Western vanity which sees itself for eternity as the sole cause of all the misfortunes of the world. The meeting of these two vanities (…) contributes to creating this super-powerful monster that is contemporary China, gorged with technology and good conscience. (…) Its hold on society aims to be total. With social credit, video surveillance, the collection of the population’s DNA, its intact will to eradicate the spiritual power of the religions that escape it, Chinese power is implementing a set of technological-political solutions capable of allowing it to realise the traditional ideal of the sovereign: while it makes itself opaque to the exterior, the exterior must be made transparent to it (…) Western modernity has become for the Chinese regime a scarecrow whose expulsion from the national community constitutes the central act of its governance. By “purifying” the Chinese political body of what comes to corrupt it from the outside, the Party reconnects, above the Chinese modernity it claims to incarnate, with the indistinctly political and religious tradition of the empire.

Emmanuel Dubois de Prisque (2022)

The tragedy of Russia lies in the fact that it has never been sufficiently autonomous and creative to build its own civilisation. At the same time, it is too vast and proud to accept a subsidiary role. On several occasions it has tried to emerge: as the “Third Rome”, as a pillar of the Orthodox faith against a Catholic and Protestant West; or as the USSR, embodying the struggle of socialism against capitalism. But these attempts have ended in failure. Consequently, the country suffers and makes others suffer, and that is the meaning of its existence, its way of reminding everyone—and itself—that it is alive. (…) All the great Russian men—writers, musicians, scientists—were formed in Europe. Russia has never accepted this dependence, which has translated, over the centuries, into rivalry and jealousy. For the German philosopher Oswald Spengler (1880–1936), the origins of this anger go back to the turn of the 17th and 18th centuries, when Tsar Peter the Great decided to open his country to Europe. He imported the best in terms of technologies, sciences, arts or education. The result, says Spengler, is that Russia was forcibly Europeanised, which created a deep and lasting resentment. In Notes from Underground, by Fyodor Dostoevsky, the narrator, locked in his basement, has a keen awareness of himself but, devoid of any artistic talent, never ceases to pour out slanders on others. For me, Putin is the reincarnation of this “underground man”. A self-assured leader who issues challenges to the world, humiliates it, but remains incapable of founding a true civilisation that other peoples would join of their own free will. (…) Building a future, improving one’s life, raising one’s children… All that must be done progressively, at the cost of important individual efforts. But Russian political culture remains very marked by the nomadic heritage, from the time when the country was dominated by the Golden Horde. Now, the raison d’être of a nomadic state is defined first of all by the conquest of new lands—Ossetia, Crimea, Donbass, and now the whole of Ukraine. This nomadic spirit is also translated by a social and psychological “chaotisation”, which prevents people from attaching themselves to places, from establishing lasting bonds. In Russia, no one feels rooted on a land. Many Russians struggle to invest in the improvement of their daily life, because they always have the feeling that tomorrow everything may collapse. In this context, the history of the last hundred years in Russia is that of a new Golden Horde, of which the current war is the latest development. (…) I am convinced that the main reason why many Russians join the army and sacrifice themselves is less material than existential, faced with the absurdity of a life devoid of any social and creative perspective. Power deliberately uses this void, this inertia to channel it towards “death for the fatherland”, what I call “necrocacy”, that is to say a system of power that is imposed on the Russian population from the cradle. Babies are dressed in military uniforms, pushchairs in the shape of tanks are manufactured, parades of child-soldiers are organised. (…) The greater the gap between the ideal and reality, the more the masses are seduced. (…) Putin’s regime has highlighted a simple thing: hatred does not need historical or universal justification. It obstinately seeks the weak points of the world order and strikes them surgically, without needing theory, proofs or ideological motivations. If Ukraine falls, Putin will not stop there. He will attack the West, beginning with Eastern Europe. He will spread, like a virus. This analogy between a virus and the Russian state is not insignificant. A virus is an entity that is both dead and alive. It is inactive when it is in a neutral state, but it activates as soon as it enters a foreign body. In the same way, the Russian state, exhausted by its long bloody history, is dead from the inside, but it comes alive when it invades another country. (…) And it is not the population that will stop Putin. Power may have destroyed all the foundations of civilisation—laws, political institutions, treaties, diplomacy, civil society and the business world—but it has not weakened; on the contrary, it has strengthened. Today, the cohesion of the population with power is almost as solid as in the Soviet era! Karl Marx, completing Hegel, wrote that history repeats itself, the first time as tragedy, the second as farce. But the farce sometimes reveals itself to be an even deeper tragedy, when it is, as in Russia, the final state of the degradation of a society.

Mikhail Epstein (2026)

“The anti-world” refers to the central concept of current Russian politics: the “Russian world” and its expansion. Initially, this idea, born in the 1990s in the circle of the philosopher Georgy Shchedrovitsky, aimed at cultural expansion. But Vladislav Surkov turned it into a propaganda weapon, expressing Russia’s desire to expand once again. What is striking is the complete emptiness of this concept. The Third Rome, the pan-Slavic project around Russia, then communism, contained a certain substance. Whereas in the Putinian version, one is in a tautology: the Russian world must expand because it is the Russian world. (…) Russia has always defined the whole world as an “anti” in relation to itself, according to the idea that it was “surrounded by enemies”: non-Christians, Catholics, Protestants, bourgeois, capitalists, imperialists, anti-Soviets, Russophobes… The image of the besieged fortress dominates recent propaganda. But this reveals that it itself is an “anti” in relation to the world. To characterise its nature as anti-West, I rely on Oswald Spengler’s famous book, The Decline of the West, where he notes that Russian civilisation was born as a pseudomorphosis, when, under Peter the Great, it took the Western historical path without being inwardly prepared for it. It assimilated and then turned everything Western against the West itself! This “pseudomorphosis” has become an “antimorphosis”. Imagine this complex, this resentment, which makes what serves as our model become precisely the source of the greatest hatred. Mimesis, mimetism, arouses Nemesis, the desire for vengeance. This is the decisive factor in all Russian politics since Peter the Great, whatever form it takes: the Russian Empire, with its desire to unite the Slavic lands against the Romance and Germanic lands, or Marxism, borrowed from the West but turned against it in order to destroy it. Russia has always borrowed from the West the theories that could serve to destroy it: Marxism, anarchism or, today, the doctrines of Guénon, Evola and other prophets of the right-wing international and Eurasianism. Putin is not an accident. He has found the sensitive point of Russian civilisation. (…) Russia resembles the “underground man” painted by Dostoevsky: incapable of creating something of its own, but sufficiently reflexive and perspicacious to mock, destroy, commit all sorts of wickedness against others and itself. With Putin, Russia behaves like the underground man. (…) The tsarist empire was also an anti-world, constantly opposing the West: with Orthodoxy against Catholicism and Protestantism; and through the progressive intelligentsia of the 19th century against bourgeois rationality. But this predator was relatively peaceful, gradually losing its fangs, ready to transform itself into a European-style state, to create a Duma… After the revolution, the opposition became more bitter, more bloody; even if elements of the Enlightenment, of rationalism, persisted in Soviet ideology. Putinism is even more aggressive. It is fanaticism that prevails, with its rhetoric of hatred and dehumanisation of the adversary. (…) certain parallels are inevitable. Russian culture carried within it the premises of the anti-world, as Thomas Mann had shown for German culture and Nazism. In the most cherished traits of Russian literature, one sometimes hears demonic resonances. (…) Just as there exists a “resource curse” of abundant resources that atrophy the capacity to work, so there exists a related territorial curse. The possession of an immense territory creates a feeling of emptiness and nomadism. Thus, sedentarised Russia has remained a nomadic “horde”. Putin calls this “restlessness”: “When everything is calm, settled, stable, one gets bored (…) one wants things to move.” Everything is said. If the “special military operation” were to end, what would one do, he even goes so far as to say? His strategy: make war, rather than set about the “boring” development of our immense land. (…) The greatest Russian writers have said it, and Andrei Platonov better than anyone. On the one hand, the manic exaltation of its leaders, the obsession with conquering the world; on the other, the fact that the more we extend this space, the more it empties and empties us ourselves. The passage from depression to obsession, and vice versa, describes the great phases of Russian history better than traditional political science: brief manic flares of the leaders, long periods of depression of the subjected people. (…) It is paradoxical but it is at the Sarov monastery, where one of the greatest Russian saints, Seraphim of Sarov, lived in asceticism, that the Federal Nuclear Centre is located. Under Patriarch Alexy, in 2007, the Church had already placed the centre under its protection, and in 2023 Patriarch Kirill declared that the nuclear weapon had been conceived in the monastery “by the ineffable Providence of God”. As if one were seeking to associate these weapons of apocalypse with sacred places. It is there that theology and the technology of the end of history meet. By continually pushing back the frontiers of emptiness, the “Russian world” risks having no other horizon than the devastation of the entire planet. (…) I repeat, Russia was projected by Peter the Great into Western history. But history is patient construction, accumulation. Apocalypse dispenses with this historical work. Everything ends immediately: paradise or hell right away. The idea of the apocalypse has always been very present in Russia; notably among the Old Believers, whose eschatology I studied in the field from the 1980s. Berdyaev also described, in The Russian Idea, the Russian people as a people of apocalypse and nihilism. The idea that Russia had been projected into History in order to put an end to it and not to succeed in it gradually became dominant with the nihilist current. For contempt for the world, for the law and for the freedoms of man, leads to the desire that everything should end as quickly as possible. (…) [Putin could use the nuclear weapon and wants to force us cynically to abandon Ukraine] Probably both. But no one, not even the underground man who sits in the Kremlin, knows at what moment this blackmail could turn into reality. Nor at what tactical or strategic level. Some say there are too many intermediate echelons for the order to go through. But we are dealing with an irrational power that has lost all sense of historical reason and that is raising the stakes in a zero-sum game that is mortally dangerous: if we cannot win, let everyone lose!

Mikhail Epstein (Emory University, Atlanta, 2026)
